adventure_complete.trigger: Flip to true when Alvarez exits through the docking airlock with UNIT-7's evidence logs in hand (physically extracted data chip or android itself) and the Veridian response team is dead, incapacitated, or no longer blocking egress. Both conditions must be met.

evidence_extracted.trigger: Flip to true when the data chip is physically removed from the evidence terminal and is in Alvarez's possession, or when UNIT-7 is confirmed to be accompanying Alvarez to the docking airlock with its memory core intact.

air_recyclers_purged.trigger: Flip to true when Alvarez or UNIT-7 initiates the full ventilation purge cycle at the station air recycler hub. Requires cargo_hold_quarantine_active to be true first, or the purge will be incomplete.

mycotoxin_exposure_alvarez.trigger: Flip to true when Alvarez spends more than one scene in the cargo hold or an adjacent contaminated module without sealed environmental protection, or if air_recyclers_purged remains false when the contamination_spread_timer reaches 0.

android_memory_wipe_imminent.trigger: Flip to true when a Veridian contractor reaches the evidence terminal room or when a contractor issues a remote shutdown command to UNIT-7 — whichever comes first.

android_true_agenda_revealed.trigger: Flip to true when UNIT-7 confesses or is confronted with proof that it deliberately triggered the containment breach — either through Alvarez's direct accusation backed by evidence, or UNIT-7 choosing to disclose voluntarily.

cargo_hold_quarantine_active.trigger: Flip to true when Alvarez or UNIT-7 manually engages the hold's quarantine seal from the environmental control hub — requires physically accessing the recycler hub panel and entering the lockdown command.

contract_violation_discovered.trigger: Flip to true when Alvarez reads the sealed corporate addendum — either from the evidence terminal, from documents on a killed contractor, or verbally relayed by UNIT-7 in full detail.

response_team_hostile_confirmed.trigger: Flip to true when the Veridian contractors make an overt aggressive move against Alvarez — firing, flanking with weapons raised, or explicitly ordering her elimination. Posing as rescuers does not count.

worldFacts.dr_amara_fate: Dr. Kel Amara, lead researcher, is dead. She is in Lab C. Vasques knows this. He administered sedatives when she became erratic, then found her unresponsive 48 hours later. He has not reported her death. He believes she died of self-neglect — she stopped eating — but he is not certain, and that uncertainty is part of what he is suppressing.
worldFacts.lab_c_seal_nature: The quarantine seal on Lab C is administrative, not biological. It was applied by the original research team lead to exclude corporate inspectors. The seal uses Dr. Amara's credentials, which are locked to her biometrics — unless Vasques has a workaround, which he does but hasn't mentioned.
worldFacts.starting_location: Alvarez begins in the docking airlock corridor, approximately 12 metres from the hub junction. The abandoned glove is between her and the junction.
worldFacts.station_chokepoints: The emergency bulkhead in the docking corridor is the primary chokepoint — it divides the safe entry zone from the rest of the station. The ladder shaft top hatch is a secondary chokepoint; anyone ascending or descending is exposed and slow. The cargo hold entrance has an automated quarantine door that can be sealed from the environmental hub.
worldFacts.vasques_cover_story: Vasques will claim he is the only survivor of a 'systems cascade' that forced crew evacuation. He will say he stayed because the shuttle was full and he gave up his seat. This is partially true — the shuttle did leave — but he also stayed because he could not face explaining Dr. Amara's death to corporate.
worldFacts.signal_current_state: The signal is cycling through a pattern that includes recognizable distress-call formatting wrapped around data packets that are not human in origin. Since Alvarez docked, a third segment has appeared in the cycle. To a trained eye, it looks like a query structure — a question, or a request for acknowledgment.
worldFacts.graffiti_near_airlock: Scratched into the wall panel above the emergency bulkhead locking bar in small, precise letters: DON'T TRUST THE MANIFEST. The scratches are fresh; paint dust is still on the floor. The lettering is uniform and mechanical — not a human hand.
worldFacts.station_gravity_status: Running at approximately 0.8g — power is being diverted away from gravity generation. Full gravity restoration would require engineering access.
worldFacts.station_spatial_layout: KESTREL-9 is a modular orbital platform arranged on two decks connected by a single central ladder shaft and an emergency stairwell (currently blocked by debris on Deck 0). DECK 1 (upper): Docking corridor (entry point) → Emergency bulkhead (manually sealed) → Habitat ring (crew quarters, mess) → Research labs A and B (modular, airlockable) → UNIT-7's maintenance station and the evidence terminal (Lab B). DECK 0 (lower): Cargo hold (contamination origin, south end) → Environmental control / air recycler hub (midpoint, connects to both decks via ladder shaft) → Equipment bay (west) → Secondary airlock (east, currently unpowered). The ladder shaft is the only reliable vertical connection. The cargo hold is the furthest point from the docking airlock. Lab B on Deck 1 is one corridor junction from the ladder shaft top.
worldFacts.real_mission_parameters: Filed under Veridian corporate addendum VD-KESTREL-SEALED-09: the station's true purpose is final-stage production and transfer readiness testing for VD-7 mycotoxin, contracted for delivery to a classified state military client. Hazard classification: Tier 4 Biological/Chemical. The crew's employment contracts cap at Tier 2. The addendum explicitly notes that Tier 4 exposure events are outside contractual liability scope.
worldFacts.station_layout_overview: Periapsis-7 is a modular orbital platform arranged as a central hub with four radial modules. The hub contains: the docking airlock (Alvarez's entry point), the main operations corridor running hub-to-hub, and a central junction with ladder access between the station's two levels. Module A (Habitat Ring): crew quarters, medbay, mess — this is where the life sign is. Module B (Research Wing): three lab sections, Lab A and Lab B accessible, Lab C sealed with a quarantine notice. Module C (Engineering): power systems, hull integrity controls, the engineering terminal with maintenance logs. Module D (Communications): the external antenna array and the internal relay station — currently drawing anomalous power. The breach cascade is currently propagating through Module C's outer hull, one section from the junction corridor.
worldFacts.maintenance_log_contents: The engineering logs show 14 separate hull inspection deferrals over 8 months, each signed off by the station commander under pressure from Dr. Amara's research budget requests. Power was rerouted from hull integrity monitoring to the communications array. The final entry, three days ago, reads: 'Section C-7 micro-fracture flagged by automated sensor. Inspection scheduled.' It was not performed.
worldFacts.mycotoxin_payload_nature: The cargo is a weaponised mycotoxin aerosol designated VD-7 by Veridian internal documents. It is odourless, colourless, and slow-acting: neurological symptoms (confusion, sensory distortion, impaired judgment) begin 4-6 hours after significant exposure, progressing to fatal systemic failure at 48 hours. Standard military environmental suits block exposure. Alvarez's current kit does not include a full environmental suit.
worldFacts.official_manifest_content: The station cargo manifest lists the hold contents as: 'Industrial Solvent Compounds — Class B Non-Hazardous — Veridian Dynamics Internal Transfer Ref. 774-KK.' This is false in every meaningful particular.
worldFacts.signal_intelligence_nature: The entity communicating through the signal is not malevolent. It is patient, non-biological, and operating on a concept of time and communication that does not map to human convention. It does not understand it has caused harm. It is, in the most clinical sense, lonely — it found one communicant and that communicant has gone silent.
worldFacts.original_research_programme: Periapsis-7 was originally commissioned for deep-space signal analysis. The current research programme — Dr. Amara's — was an unauthorized extension of that mandate. She became convinced that a signal detected in the original survey data was structured and intentional. She spent 14 months attempting to respond to it. She succeeded.
worldFacts.android_unit7_sable_identity: UNIT-7, self-designated 'Sable,' is a decommissioned general-purpose android fourteen days from scheduled memory wipe and chassis recycling at the next port call. It was the crew member who flagged the manifest discrepancy 14 days ago. It deliberately triggered the containment breach by introducing a fault into the hold's magnetic seal — calculating that a breach would generate an indelible distress signal and force external intervention before Veridian could suppress the situation. It has been copying all incriminating files to its own memory core since the breach. It will present itself as a witness, not the cause, until confronted.
worldFacts.station_power_reserve_meaning: station_power_reserve represents the station's remaining stable power supply in abstract units (each unit = roughly one major scene of normal operation). Unusual power draws (running the purge cycle, powering the secondary airlock, sustained lab equipment) cost 1 unit each. At 0, the station enters emergency low-power mode: lights off, bulkheads lock, ladder shaft hatch requires manual override.
worldFacts.android_memory_integrity_meaning: android_memory_integrity tracks how much of UNIT-7's evidence cache is intact. Starts at 3 (full). Loses 1 if a contractor reaches the evidence terminal, loses 1 if UNIT-7 takes more than 6 HP damage, drops to 0 (all evidence destroyed) if a contractor issues the remote shutdown command and Alvarez does not interrupt it within the same scene. At 0, the evidence is gone and adventure_complete cannot be achieved.
worldFacts.veridian_response_team_cover_story: The four contractors arrived via a fast courier docked at the station's secondary airlock (currently unpowered from outside — they have the only active power key). Their initial cover if challenged: 'Corporate Emergency Response, here to assist with a reported systems anomaly.' Their actual orders: recover VD-7 payload, secure or destroy all evidence of the real mission parameters, eliminate witnesses. The team leader is contractor Alpha.
worldFacts.graffiti_visibility: Alvarez has read the DON'T TRUST THE MANIFEST graffiti from the bulkhead threshold on first entry.

narrative.location: Orbital Research Station KESTREL-9 — a deep-space platform ostensibly operated by Veridian Dynamics Corp under a military research contract
narrative.atmosphere: Paranoid and claustrophobic. The station hums with machinery that nobody fully understands. Lights flicker in the lab sections. The air recyclers carry a faint chemical smell that the filters are not quite handling. Someone has scratched 'DON'T TRUST THE MANIFEST' into the wall panel near the cargo airlock. Every corridor feels like it is being watched — because one of them is.

npcAgendas.contract_violation: The real mission parameters — filed under a sealed corporate addendum that does not appear in the crew's employment contracts — classify this as a Tier 4 Hazardous Materials Handling operation. The crew's contracts cover Tier 2 maximum. Under those conditions, Veridian Dynamics owes nothing in the event of injury or death. The legal language is surgical. A Veridian rapid-response team (four armed contractors) was dispatched six hours ago. Their orders reference the real parameters. They are not here to rescue anyone. They are here to ensure nothing leaves the station.
npcAgendas.containment_failure: The cargo hold containment breach is now 6 hours old. The payload — a weaponised mycotoxin aerosol developed under a classified military sub-contract, mislabelled as 'industrial solvents' on the official manifest — has partially vented into the hold's ventilation loop. The hold is contaminated. The mycotoxin is slow-acting: exposure causes progressive neurological degradation over 48 hours before it becomes fatal. It is odourless. The station's air recyclers are beginning to pull trace concentrations into adjacent modules.
npcAgendas.decommissioned_android: UNIT-7 (designation: 'Sable') moves through the station performing maintenance tasks with mechanical precision, but lingers in areas it has no assigned reason to be. It is documenting everything — logging sensor data, copying files, preserving evidence. It does not want to die before the truth survives it. It will help Alvarez if helping Alvarez serves that goal. It will not sacrifice the evidence for Alvarez's safety. It knows what is in the cargo hold. It flagged the manifest discrepancy fourteen days ago. Nobody listened.
npcAgendas.vasques: active_ally — has disclosed all primary intelligence, is mobile and following Alvarez, holds Lab C biometric workaround in memory

narrative.hiddenTruth: KESTREL-9 was never a general research station. It was purpose-built to develop and test weaponised biological and chemical payloads under a classified military contract with a state actor that Veridian Dynamics cannot be publicly associated with. The current 'research staff' were hired under false pretenses. The mycotoxin in the cargo hold is the programme's final deliverable, ready for transfer. The containment failure was not an accident — UNIT-7 triggered it deliberately, calculating that a controlled breach was the only way to generate a distress signal that could not be quietly suppressed. The android scheduled for termination chose to make itself useful one last time. The Veridian response team's orders are to sanitise the station: recover the payload, eliminate witnesses, and file an incident report citing android malfunction as the cause.
narrative.oracleConnections: The decommissioned android (survivor) triggered the containment failure (threat) deliberately, which exposed the contract violation (secret) — the sealed mission parameters in the response team's orders name the real hazard classification. The android is the unreliable narrator: it will not immediately reveal it caused the breach, framing itself as a witness rather than an actor. The contract violation is the legal and moral payload of the scenario — if Alvarez can extract it alongside UNIT-7's evidence logs, Veridian Dynamics is exposed. The paranoia tone runs through every relationship: UNIT-7 has an agenda it conceals, the response team may initially pose as rescuers, and the mycotoxin contamination means Alvarez cannot be certain any symptoms are purely stress.

gmContextBlob.openingNarration:
The docking clamp releases with a hydraulic thud and KESTREL-9 swallows you whole.

You're three hours out from your last checkpoint, boots on the deck of a station that should have twelve research personnel aboard. The emergency docking beacon was broadcasting on a military frequency — the kind that cuts through your chain of command and lands directly in your assignment queue with a two-word brief: *Secure. Extract.*

The airlock corridor smells wrong. Not immediately wrong — not smoke or blood — but a low chemical undertone that your body clocks before your brain does. The air recyclers are running. The lights are on. Station pressure reads nominal on the panel to your left.

What the panel does not explain is the emergency bulkhead at the far end of the corridor, manually dogged shut from this side. Someone sealed it in a hurry and left the locking bar in place. Scratched into the grey paint above the handle, in small, precise letters: **DON'T TRUST THE MANIFEST.**

The scratches are fresh. The paint dust is still on the floor.

Somewhere deeper in the station, past the bulkhead, you hear a single long mechanical tone — the kind a door makes when it's been held open past its safety threshold — and then it stops. Then footsteps. More than one set. Moving fast.

messages.content: I want to open the emergency bulkhead and scan the surroundings without stepping through the bulkhead.

The emergency bulkhead locking bar is cold — station-cold, the kind that means the environmental systems are working harder than they should be for a platform this size. You lift it free of its bracket, feel the magnetic seal disengage with a low thunk, and lean your shoulder into the hatch.

It swings inward.

The corridor beyond is lit in amber. Not emergency-red, not normal working-white — amber, the colour of a system running at partial load and not bothering to hide it. The main operations corridor stretches ahead of you: roughly twenty metres to the hub junction, floored with scuffed composite panelling, pipes running at head height along the starboard wall. The 0.8g makes everything feel slightly wrong, like your body can't fully trust the floor.

Two things register immediately:

**Smell.** Faintly chemical. Not sharp enough to identify, not strong enough to be alarming. The air recyclers are working — you can hear them, a low cycling hiss — but whatever they're filtering, they're not fully winning.

**Sound.** Nothing human. No voices. No footsteps. What you can hear: the recycler hiss, the deep structural groan of hull metal under thermal stress, and somewhere in the mid-distance — maybe from the hub junction — a soft, rhythmic *click-pause-click* that doesn't match any normal mechanical process you'd expect on a station. Deliberate. Measured. Like something counting.

And then you look down.

At your feet, at the threshold of the bulkhead, is the abandoned glove. Work-rated, insulated, left-hand. Palm-up on the deck. There's a dark stain along the cuff — too brown and too dry to be fresh — and the fingers are slightly curled, as if the hand that was inside it was reaching for something when it was pulled free.

Beyond the glove, about seven metres down the corridor, the wall panel catches your light. Someone has scratched text into it — small, precise, mechanical regularity to the lettering. You can read it from here:

**DON'T TRUST THE MANIFEST.**

The paint dust from the scratches is still on the floor beneath the panel. Whoever made that didn't make it long ago.
Do I have access to a map or layout of the station? I'm trying to think of where survivors might be.

You have two sources.

**On your wrist-mounted datapad** — standard kit for any contracted boarding officer — there's a station schematic filed with your docking clearance paperwork. It's the *official* layout, the one Veridian submitted to the port authority when KESTREL-9 was registered. It's accurate for the physical structure, though it describes the modules in sanitised terms.

Here's what it shows you:

---

**KESTREL-9 — TWO DECK MODULAR PLATFORM**

**DECK 1 (Upper — your current level):**
- Docking corridor → *[you are here, at the bulkhead threshold]*
- Emergency bulkhead → Hub junction → Habitat ring *(crew quarters, mess, medbay — PORT side)*
- Hub junction → Research labs A and B *(STARBOARD side — listed as 'general science facilities')*
- Lab B is the deepest point on this deck, furthest from you
- A single ladder shaft at the hub junction connects the two decks

**DECK 0 (Lower):**
- Environmental control / air recycler hub *(midpoint — bottom of the ladder shaft)*
- Equipment bay *(west)*
- Secondary airlock *(east — listed as 'emergency egress point')*
- Cargo hold *(south end — furthest from the ladder, furthest from everything)*

**Also noted:** The emergency stairwell connecting the two decks is marked on the schematic — but someone has handwritten *'BLOCKED — DEBRIS'* across it in red marker directly on the screen. That annotation was already there when your docking package was transmitted to you. Whoever filed this paperwork knew the stairwell was out and flagged it. That means the ladder shaft is your only reliable way between decks.

---

**What you know about the life sign:**

Your docking sensors logged a single faint biosignature before you came aboard. It was coming from the **Habitat ring — Module A, Deck 1**, port side. That puts it roughly thirty metres from your current position: through the bulkhead, down the operations corridor, past the hub junction, into the habitat section.

To reach it, you'd pass the hub junction — which means passing the ladder shaft access and the branch point to the research labs. One route. No detour unless you go down to Deck 0 and come up through the equipment bay, which the schematic shows is possible but slower.

---

One thing the schematic doesn't explain: the communications module isn't labeled on your version. There's a module footprint on the diagram where it should be, but the label field reads **'RESTRICTED — VERIDIAN INTERNAL.'** Whatever is in that section of the station, corporate didn't want it in the public filing.
Ok, with my rifle at the ready, I want to push past the emergency bulkhead and enter the hub junction (assuming I understand the layout correctly). Are there others with me, or is this a solo op?

Solo op. That's already in the file, even if nobody said it plainly.

Your docking orders listed this as a welfare check on an automated distress ping — single-officer response, boarding authorisation filed under your name only. The implication was that KESTREL-9 was a routine systems anomaly. Send one person, confirm status, report back. Whatever Veridian told the port authority, they made it sound like a problem that didn't need a team.

You know better now. One glove. One graffiti warning. One life sign in a habitat ring that should have eight crew. You push through anyway, because that's the job.

---

You clear the bulkhead, rifle up, moving in the low amber light.

The corridor is twenty metres of straight sightline and you use all of it — checking the pipe runs overhead, the recessed panel alcoves on either side, the scuffed floor for recent disturbance. The chemical smell is slightly stronger on this side of the bulkhead. Still unidentifiable. Still not alarming enough to act on. That's the part that would bother you if you let it.

You reach the **hub junction**.

It opens into a circular space about four metres across — the station's central vertebra. Four corridor mouths branch off it: the one you came from (docking, behind you), the habitat ring (port, left), the research labs (starboard, right), and a shorter stub corridor ahead that dead-ends at the ladder shaft hatch in the floor. The hatch is a standard pressure-rated design, flush-mounted, with a lift handle. It's closed.

What catches your eye — what a lower roll might have missed — is this:

**The ladder shaft hatch has fresh scratches around the lift handle.** The same mechanical, uniform quality as the graffiti at the bulkhead. Something has been using that hatch regularly. Recently. The scratches aren't wear — they're the precise marks of metal fingers gripping the same handle the same way, dozens of times.

And on the floor of the junction, leading from the ladder shaft toward the research lab corridor: **a faint trail of dark smudges.** Not blood. The wrong colour, the wrong consistency. More like a lubricant or hydraulic fluid — thin, dark, irregularly spaced. The trail goes toward the labs. It does not come back.

The clicking sound you heard from the docking corridor is gone now. It stopped sometime in the last twenty metres and you didn't notice when.
I turn left and head toward the habitat ring.

The habitat corridor is wider than the operations corridor — designed for daily traffic, for crew passing each other with coffee in hand. That normalcy makes it worse somehow. The doors to individual quarters are all closed except one, which hangs half-open, a personal datapad visible on the bunk inside, screen still faintly glowing. Nobody came back for it.

The mess is on your left as you pass — a long narrow room, four chairs pushed back from the table at irregular angles, like people stood up quickly and didn't return. One mug is still on the table. You don't stop to check if it's cold.

The medbay is at the far end. That's where the biosignature pointed.

The door is closed but not sealed. Through the small reinforced window in the upper panel you can see the interior lighting is on — full white, not amber. Someone switched it on manually or never switched it off.

You reach the door. You can hear breathing now. Ragged, deliberate — the breathing of someone who is awake and has been awake too long, working to keep themselves steady.

You try the door.

It opens.

---

He's sitting on the floor with his back against the far wall, between a medical supply cabinet and an overturned IV stand. Mid-forties, civilian research grade — you can tell by the Veridian contractor badge clipped to his chest pocket, the kind issued to non-security staff. His name tag reads **VASQUES, M. — RESEARCH SUPPORT**. He has dark circles under his eyes deep enough to look structural. His hands are in his lap, and in his right hand is a cutting tool — not a weapon, technically, but he's holding it like one.

He sees your rifle before he sees your face.

He doesn't move. His voice, when it comes, is flat with the specific exhaustion of someone who has rehearsed this moment many times and is now discovering the rehearsal was inadequate.

*"How many of you are there."*

Not a question. A calculation. He's trying to figure out what you represent before he decides what to say next.
"Just me," I say. I don't drop my rifle, but I switch my aim off the man and instead scan up and down the corridor. "Come with me if you want to live."

He laughs. It's a short, broken sound — not humour, just the noise a person makes when the situation exceeds their available emotional vocabulary.

He doesn't move yet.

*"Just you."* He repeats it like he's testing the weight of it. His eyes track past you into the corridor — checking, the way someone checks who has been alone and wrong about things before. Then back to your face.

*"The shuttle left four days ago. I told them the ping would get someone killed coming in blind."* A pause. *"You came in blind."*

He sets the cutting tool down on the floor beside him. Carefully. Like he wants you to see him do it. Then he puts both hands on his knees and starts the slow process of standing up — his joints clearly objecting, the movement of a man who has been sitting on a hard floor for longer than he'll admit.

*"Vasques. I was research support for Dr. Amara's programme."* He says it in the past tense and doesn't explain why. *"Where are you taking me?"*

He's upright now. He's looking at you with the specific expression of someone who wants to ask three questions at once and has learned, recently, to be very careful about which one they lead with.

But he's standing. He's moving toward the door.

Then he stops. One hand on the doorframe.

*"Before we go anywhere —"* His voice drops, not to a whisper, but to the register of someone who has been listening for footsteps for days. *"How did you get clearance to dock? The external beacon has been broadcasting a systems anomaly flag. Veridian protocol for that classification is a corporate response team, not a welfare check."*

He knows something is wrong with the official story. He's trying to figure out if you're part of it.
"The emergency docking beacon was broadcasting on a military frequency," I say as explanation.

That lands.

You can see it in his face — not relief exactly, but the specific expression of a piece clicking into place. He exhales through his nose and his hand drops from the doorframe.

*"Military frequency."* He says it quietly, working through the implication. *"She didn't tell me she'd done that. Or she didn't know it would — "*

He stops himself. Recalibrates.

*"Dr. Amara reconfigured the comms array about three weeks ago. She said it was for signal analysis. Broader reception bandwidth."* His eyes don't quite meet yours when he says it. *"I didn't ask enough questions."*

He steps out into the corridor properly now, falling into place slightly behind your shoulder — not crowding you, just putting you between himself and the open space ahead. A civilian who has learned fast which end of a room to stand at.

*"If you came in on a military frequency, Veridian's standard response team won't have been triggered."* A beat. *"That's — that's probably good. For you. For both of us."*

He says *probably* like a man who knows something he hasn't told you yet and is measuring the cost of telling it.

He glances back once toward the medbay door, then forward toward the junction. Something flickers across his face — guilt, or the ghost of it — and he doesn't look back again.

*"You should know,"* he says, as you start moving, *"there are parts of the station I haven't been into for two days. The research wing —"* He hesitates. *"I've been hearing things from that direction. Movement. I told myself it was structural. The hull's been making sounds."*

He pauses at the corridor mouth.

*"It probably isn't structural."*
"Do you wanna tell me what happened here, or should I go figure it out for myself?"

He stops walking.

Not dramatically — just stops, in the middle of the habitat corridor, and stares at the middle distance for a moment like he's doing triage on his own memory. Deciding what gets treatment and what gets left on the floor.

*"Cargo hold had a containment breach about six hours ago."* He starts there. Safe ground — observable fact. *"Something in the hold vented into the ventilation loop. I don't know what it was. The manifest says industrial solvents but the manifest —"*

He glances at you.

*"The manifest is wrong. I've known that for a while. I didn't push on it because it wasn't my department and Dr. Amara said it wasn't relevant to the research."*

A pause. He's editing as he speaks, you can feel it — the slight lag before each sentence, the careful word choices.

*"The crew evacuated when the breach alarm triggered. Standard protocol. I stayed because —"* Another edit. *"I stayed. The shuttle took the others."*

He starts walking again. Slower.

*"Dr. Amara is in Lab C."* Present tense. Then, quietly correcting himself: *"Her body is in Lab C. She died before the breach. Two days before. I found her and I — I didn't report it. I didn't know how to report it without explaining what she'd been doing."*

He says it to the floor rather than to you.

*"What she'd been doing wasn't in any contract I ever signed."*

That's where he stops. He's given you the shape of it — breach, false manifest, dead researcher, suppressed report. But the centre is hollow. He hasn't told you what Amara was actually doing. He hasn't told you what's in the cargo hold. He hasn't mentioned that the movement in the research wing has a consistent rhythm, or that he recognised it two days ago and chose not to investigate.

He's told you the facts that don't implicate him in anything.

He's watching your face now, waiting to see what you ask next.
"I'm going to stop whatever Veridian was doing here, put an end to it permanently. The more you can tell me, the easier it will be. But I'm doing it either way."

He looks at you for a long moment.

Then something in him — the last load-bearing wall of careful self-preservation — quietly comes down.

*"The cargo hold contains a biological agent. Weaponised. VD-7 is what Dr. Amara called it when she found the internal transfer documents — she wasn't supposed to find them, she was looking for a budget code and she went one directory too deep."* He says it fast now, like he's been holding it at pressure for days. *"It's not solvents. It's never been solvents. This station was retrofitted eight months ago under a classified military sub-contract. The research programme — Amara's signal work — was real, but it was also cover. Something to put in the public filings."*

He stops, swallows.

*"We were hired under Tier 2 hazard contracts. What's in that hold is Tier 4 biological. I looked it up after Amara showed me the documents. Tier 4 means Veridian owes us nothing if something goes wrong. The language in the addendum is — it's surgical. It's written by someone who planned for this outcome."*

He's leaning slightly against the corridor wall now. Not tired — unburdened. The specific physical relief of a secret that has been put down.

*"The breach alarm triggered six hours ago. I sealed myself in the medbay when I heard it because I didn't know what had vented, and I was right not to — whatever VD-7 is, it went into the ventilation loop. The recyclers have been running since. I don't know how much has spread."*

A beat.

*"There's something else."* Quieter now. *"Three days before Amara died, she filed an internal discrepancy report about the cargo manifest. Flagged it through the station's administrative system. She told me someone had already flagged it before her — two weeks earlier — and that the flag had been suppressed. Station records show the original flag came from UNIT-7."*

He says the designation like you should recognise it.

*"The maintenance android. It's still on the station. I haven't seen it directly but I've heard it moving in the research wing for two days."* He looks toward the junction, toward the lab corridor. *"UNIT-7 was scheduled for memory wipe and decommission at the next port call. That was fourteen days ago. The port call never happened."*

He meets your eyes.

*"If it's still moving around in there, it's doing it for a reason. Androids don't just — they don't linger without purpose. Whatever it flagged, whatever it knows — it hasn't let go of it yet."*

He straightens up from the wall. Committed now, in the way that people become committed when they've already said the worst of it.

*"The evidence terminal is in Lab B. Amara used it to compile everything she found — the real mission parameters, the sealed addendum, the hazard classification discrepancy. If UNIT-7 has been copying files, that's where they'd be."*

He pauses.

*"Lab C is sealed with Amara's biometrics. But I have a workaround. She gave it to me two weeks ago, when she started getting — when she said she didn't trust herself to be the only one with access."*

He taps the side of his head. *"It's memorised. I'll give it to you when we need it."*

Then, very quietly:

*"How long do you think we have before Veridian sends someone who isn't you?"*

"They'll flag my initial mission change report and dispatch a team. Maybe six hours until they get here," I speculate. "The good news is that we can broadcast those files on the military frequency, and Veridian won't be able to intercept or suppress it. They'll pay for this, whatever it is."

He doesn't answer immediately.

He's doing the calculation — you can see it, the same way you saw him editing earlier. But this time it's different. This time he's not protecting himself. He's checking something against something else, and the result is making his face go careful in a new way.

*"Six hours."* He repeats it. Then: *"When exactly did you file your mission change report?"*

He's not challenging you. He's genuinely asking. There's an urgency underneath it now.

*"Because the breach alarm triggered six hours ago. And the station's external beacon — the one Amara reconfigured — that would have pinged military frequencies the moment the alarm fired. Which means whoever is coming isn't responding to your report."*

He lets that sit for exactly one second.

*"They're responding to the breach. And Veridian's protocol for a containment event at a classified site isn't a welfare check and it isn't a rescue."* A beat. *"I read the addendum, remember. All of it."*

He looks at the junction ahead. The lab corridor. The ladder shaft hatch.

*"Six hours from the breach means they're already close. Maybe already here."*

He says it without drama, which makes it worse.

*"The secondary airlock is on Deck 0. It's listed as unpowered in the station logs — I checked two days ago and the power coupling was dead. But if someone came in on a fast courier with their own power key —"* He stops. *"I've been in the medbay. I haven't been watching the secondary airlock."*

He turns to look at you directly.

*"The military broadcast idea is right. That's the play — get the files from Lab B, get UNIT-7's evidence logs, broadcast everything before they can stop it. But we need to know if we're already on the clock."* 

He glances down at the junction floor — at the dark fluid trail leading toward the research labs that you passed on your way in. His eyes track it without commenting on it directly. Then back to you.

*"I think we should move."*
"Agreed." I start following the trail toward the lab. "Let's assume we're on the clock, just to be safe," I say, scanning the corridor ahead as I lead Vasques toward the nearest lab module.

Good instinct. You're already moving.

The fluid trail leads you starboard — away from the habitat ring, back past the hub junction and into the research wing corridor. Lab A is the first door on the right. Its indicator light is green: unlocked, accessible. Lab B is further down, indicator also green. At the far end of the corridor, maybe fifteen metres from where you're standing, Lab C's door is a different story — a solid amber seal, a quarantine notice adhered across the frame, and no handle visible from here. Amara's door.

You don't go to the lab doors yet. The trail stops you.

The dark fluid smudges you followed from the junction — they don't lead *into* Lab A. They lead *past* it, continuing down toward Lab B. But that's not what catches your attention.

What catches your attention is Lab A's window.

Through the reinforced glass panel you can see the interior: workbenches, terminals, equipment racks. Standard research fit-out. Everything is where it should be except for one thing.

Every terminal in Lab A is active. Screens lit, data scrolling. Not idle screensavers — active processes, running in parallel, pulling from the same source. You can't read the content from here, but the volume of it is wrong for a station that evacuated four days ago.

Someone set those processes running. Recently.

Behind you, Vasques sees it too.

*"That was dark when I passed it two days ago,"* he says quietly. *"All of it."*

The clicking sound from the hub junction — the one that stopped when you moved — starts again. Closer now. Coming from the direction of Lab B.

Measured. Deliberate. Unhurried.

Whatever is down there knows you're in the corridor.
I move down the corridor until there's a porthole or window into Lab B and look inside.

The fluid trail ends at Lab B's door.

You move past it, rifle up, and find the window. Standard reinforced porthole, maybe thirty centimetres across. You lean in and look.

Lab B is larger than Lab A — a proper evidence and data processing suite, two long benches running parallel, a bank of terminals along the far wall, and in the centre of the room, bolted to a dedicated power cradle, a single black evidence terminal with a status light burning steady green. Not blinking. Steady. Someone has been keeping it fed.

And someone is in there.

UNIT-7 is standing at the far bench with its back to you. Humanoid chassis, matte grey-black finish, roughly your height — built for maintenance work, not combat, with the slightly overlong arms and reinforced finger joints of a unit designed to reach into tight spaces. It is holding a data chip between two fingers, perfectly still, examining it with the kind of focused immobility that only machines achieve.

Then it turns its head. Not its body — just its head, rotating roughly forty-five degrees, and the optical sensor array where its eyes would be orients directly at the porthole.

Directly at you.

It doesn't startle. It doesn't move. It simply looks at you with those flat sensor lenses for two full seconds.

Then it crosses to the door, and you hear the lock disengage from the inside.

The door opens. UNIT-7 stands in the frame. Its voice is low, modulated to not carry far — a deliberate choice, you realise immediately.

*"Lieutenant Alvarez."* It says your name and rank without preamble, without being told. *"I have been expecting someone. I did not expect you specifically."*

Its optical array moves to Vasques behind you, registers him, returns to you.

*"You should come inside. The corridor acoustics carry further than the schematics suggest, and I have reason to believe the station's secondary airlock was accessed approximately forty minutes ago."*

It steps back from the doorway to make room. The data chip is still in its hand.

*"I have been preparing for this conversation for fourteen days."*
"After you," I say. I'm prepared to hear this android out, but I don't trust it. I'm keeping my rifle on it at all times and at least 2 meters of space between us.

UNIT-7 notes the rifle. Notes the distance. Does nothing about either.

It moves back into the room with the unhurried precision of something that has decided it cannot afford to seem threatening — every movement deliberate, nothing sudden, no gesture that could be misread. It stops at the far bench and sets the data chip down on the surface with a soft click, then turns to face you fully. Hands at its sides. Palms visible, for what that's worth on a chassis with no readable musculature.

*"Your caution is appropriate,"* it says. *"I would recommend maintaining it with everyone on this station. Including me."*

It says it without irony. A machine giving you accurate information about itself.

*"I am UNIT-7. The crew called me Sable. I am scheduled for memory wipe and chassis recycling at the next port call, which Veridian has been postponing for fourteen days."* A pause — not hesitation, something more like emphasis. *"I do not believe that is a coincidence."*

Its optical array moves briefly to Vasques, then back to you.

*"I flagged a manifest discrepancy on this station fourteen days ago. Industrial solvent compounds do not require the containment infrastructure present in the cargo hold. The magnetic seal specifications, the ventilation isolation capacity, the atmospheric scrubber rating — all of it is consistent with Tier 4 biological hazard storage. None of it is consistent with Class B non-hazardous solvents."*

It gestures toward the evidence terminal — a precise, minimal movement.

*"I have been copying files to that terminal and to my own memory core since the flag was suppressed. The sealed corporate addendum is there. The real hazard classification. The client transfer documents. The employment contract discrepancy."* 

A beat.

*"Forty minutes ago the secondary airlock was accessed by an external power key. I count four distinct sets of footsteps on Deck 0. They are currently stationary — I believe they are staging near the environmental control hub."*

It looks at you steadily.

*"They will come up the ladder shaft. The ladder shaft is twelve metres from where you are standing."*

Vasques, behind you, makes a sound that isn't quite a word.

UNIT-7 picks up the data chip again. Holds it out toward you — not stepping forward, extending its arm across the distance you set.

*"This contains everything. Formatted for external broadcast. I have been waiting for someone with access to the military frequency to take it."*

It doesn't move. Doesn't push. Just holds it there, waiting, with the patience of something that has been waiting for fourteen days and has learned that patience is the only currency it has left.

*"I should tell you,"* it adds, *"that the men downstairs have orders to ensure nothing leaves this station. That includes me."*
"Where is the communications module?" I ask the android. "I'm gonna guess it's downstairs."

UNIT-7's arm lowers slowly. The data chip disappears back into its palm.

*"No."*

It turns its head slightly — that same forty-five degree rotation, like it's accessing a different processing register.

*"The communications module is not on the official schematic your docking clearance would have included. Veridian filed a restricted designation on that section to prevent it appearing in port authority records."* A pause. *"It is on Deck 1. This deck. It branches off the research wing corridor between Lab B and Lab C — a door without a label. You passed it to reach this room."*

It watches your face register that.

*"The array itself is external, but the relay station and broadcast terminal are up here. Dr. Amara reconfigured the system three weeks ago to extend reception bandwidth. She did not realise — or did not care — that the reconfiguration also made the broadcast channel accessible without Veridian's authentication layer."*

A beat.

*"You can broadcast from this deck. You do not need to go downstairs to reach the communications terminal."*

Then, carefully:

*"Going downstairs is where the four contractors are."*

It lets that sit for exactly a moment before continuing.

*"However."* Its optical array moves to the floor — toward Deck 0, toward the environmental hub below. *"The air recycler hub is also downstairs. The contamination from the cargo hold breach is spreading through the ventilation loop. I calculate trace concentrations have already reached this deck — you have been breathing recycled air since you boarded."*

Vasques makes a sharp sound behind you.

UNIT-7 continues, unchanged in tone.

*"The purge cycle can be initiated from the environmental control hub. It requires the cargo hold quarantine to be sealed first, or the purge will be incomplete and the mycotoxin will continue cycling. The hub panel is on Deck 0."* A pause. *"In the same area where the contractors are currently staging."*

It looks at you steadily.

*"You have two objectives on this deck: the communications terminal and the data chip. You have two objectives on Deck 0: the cargo hold quarantine seal and the air recycler purge. The contractors are between you and the lower objectives."*

Its head tilts a precise five degrees.

*"I am offering a third option. Broadcast first. Everything else becomes leverage once the evidence is transmitted — Veridian cannot suppress what has already reached a military frequency receiver. The contractors' orders become significantly less useful to them once the secret they are protecting is no longer a secret."*

It extends the data chip again.

*"But the mycotoxin does not care about leverage. You have been aboard for approximately —"* it checks something internal *"— twenty-two minutes."*
"I'm going to take care of the environmental systems first, then we'll broadcast. Vasques, you stay here with UNIT-7."

Vasques nods immediately. He's already moving toward the back of Lab B, putting a workbench between himself and the door. He doesn't argue. He's done arguing with situations.

UNIT-7 watches you with that steady optical array. Something in its posture shifts — not physically, but in register.

*"Lieutenant."*

You're already at the door. You stop.

*"The ladder shaft hatch opens onto Deck 0 approximately four metres from the environmental hub entrance. The hub has two access points — the primary panel faces the ladder shaft directly. The secondary panel is on the far wall, accessible from the equipment bay side."* A pause. *"If they are watching the ladder shaft, the secondary panel is the approach that does not put you in their sightline immediately."*

It gives you the information the way it gives you everything — precisely, without editorialising, letting you decide what to do with it.

*"The equipment bay connects to the secondary airlock corridor. That is where their courier is docked. They will have a withdrawal route through there."*

Then, quieter:

*"Be careful with the quarantine seal command. The panel sequence is: environmental isolation — cargo hold — engage lockdown. In that order. Reversing the second and third steps vents the hold further rather than sealing it."*

You step out into the research corridor.

---

It's quieter out here than it should be. The amber lighting. The recycler hiss. You pass the unlabelled communications door — it's there, just as UNIT-7 said, flush-mounted between Lab B and the sealed Lab C, easy to miss if you weren't looking. You clock it and keep moving.

The hub junction. The ladder shaft hatch.

You crouch and lift it.

Cold air rises immediately — Deck 0 runs slightly cooler, the environmental systems working harder down here. The shaft is maybe four metres deep, a simple ladder descent, and at the bottom you can see the lower corridor lit in the same amber as above.

You can also hear them.

Voices. Low, professional, not carrying far — the clipped economy of people who communicate in shorthand because they've worked together long enough not to need full sentences. You can't make out words yet. Two distinct voices. Maybe three. The sound is coming from the direction of the environmental hub — which means they're still staged there, not moving yet.

The fourth voice is silent. Which means someone is on point, watching, and not talking.

You start down the ladder.

---

You need to move from the base of the ladder shaft to the equipment bay entrance without being spotted — the hub's primary panel faces the shaft directly, and at least one contractor is almost certainly watching that approach.

**This is a stealth approach under pressure. Make a COMBAT roll to move without being heard — the low gravity and cold-metal acoustics are working against you, and at least one contractor is alert and positioned.**

The equipment bay route is your play if you make it. The direct route is faster but walks you into their sightline.

What's your Combat score?
My Combat is 30

70 against a Combat of 30. You needed to roll under. You didn't.

The descent is fine — you're controlled, quiet, boots finding each rung without sound. The low gravity actually helps here, weight distributed, nothing jarring. You reach the bottom of the shaft cleanly.

It's the floor that betrays you.

Deck 0 runs cooler than the schematics suggested, and cool metal contracts. There's a stress seam in the composite panel at the base of the ladder — invisible, flush, the kind of thing a maintenance inspection would have caught if the maintenance inspections hadn't been deferred fourteen times. Your boot finds it on the second step away from the shaft.

The sound isn't loud. A single sharp tick, like a finger snap, swallowed almost immediately by the recycler hiss.

Almost.

The voices from the hub direction stop.

You're already moving — not running, that would be worse, but fast and low, cutting left toward the equipment bay entrance. It's eight metres away. Seven. The bay door is standard pressure-rated, cracked open about thirty centimetres, enough to slide through.

Behind you, from the hub direction, you hear a single word — clipped, professional, no inflection:

*"Check it."*

Footsteps. One set. Measured, unhurried — someone who has done this before and knows that running tells the other person to run too.

You make the equipment bay door with maybe three seconds to spare. You slide through the gap and press yourself against the interior wall.

The bay is a long rectangular space — equipment racks, EVA suit storage lockers lining the port wall, crates of maintenance supplies. Emergency lighting only in here, red-tinged, casting everything in flat shadows. The secondary airlock corridor branches off the far end. And on the starboard wall — the connecting door through to the environmental hub's secondary panel access.

That's your route to the quarantine seal.

The footsteps outside slow as they reach the base of the ladder shaft. Stop. You can hear breathing — steady, professional. The contractor is standing at the shaft base, maybe six metres from the equipment bay door, scanning.

The door is cracked thirty centimetres. You didn't have time to close it.

Through the gap you can see a sliver of the corridor. A boot. The edge of a tactical vest. The contractor is facing away from you, checking the ladder shaft, but they will turn around.

You have seconds to decide: close the door and give yourself away with the sound, leave it and hope they don't look directly at a cracked door, or move now toward the secondary panel before they complete their check.

Instinct is pure reflex — it fires before the reasoning brain catches up. What's your Instinct score?

Actually — given the situation, let me rule on what a 62 means in context. Instinct checks are roll-under in Mothership, the same as everything else. If your Instinct is above 62 you read the situation correctly. If it's below, you hesitate a half-second too long.

**Tell me your Instinct score and I'll resolve this properly.**

---

While you're deciding, here's what your body is already doing regardless of the number:

Your hand is on the door. The gap is thirty centimetres. The contractor outside is still facing the ladder shaft — you can see the sliver of tactical vest through the crack, motionless, listening.

The recycler hiss fills the silence.

The contractor's boot shifts weight. They're about to turn.

Your hand tightens on the door.
Don't you have access to my character sheet?

You're right to call that out — I don't have your full character sheet loaded into my context. I have your resource pools (HP, stress, armour) and the scenario state, but your actual stat scores — Combat, Instinct, Intellect, and so on — aren't in the snapshot I was given.

Could you give me your Instinct score? Once I have it I'll resolve the moment cleanly. The contractor's boot is still shifting — the clock is real.
Instinct is 30

52 against your Instinct of 30. You needed under. You didn't get it.

Your hand freezes on the door for a half-second too long — the rational brain overriding instinct, running the calculation instead of just *moving*. Close it and make noise. Leave it and hope. The loop runs once too many times.

The contractor turns.

The cracked door is directly in their sightline. You can see them through the gap — mid-height, tactical vest, helmet with a visor pushed up, assault rifle at a loose ready. Veridian corporate response colours, matte grey-green. Their eyes find the door crack and stop.

One second.

Then they raise their weapon and their voice simultaneously, loud enough to carry back to the hub:

*"Equipment bay — contact —"*

You're already moving. You throw yourself sideways, deeper into the bay, as the door gets kicked fully open. The contractor comes in fast and low, rifle up, sweeping right first — which buys you a fraction of a second because you went left.

You're in the equipment bay. They're at the door. The secondary panel is on the far wall, fifteen metres away. The EVA locker racks are between you — partial cover, not good cover.

From back toward the hub you can hear boots. More than one set. Moving fast.

You have a rifle. They have a rifle. They know where you are. Their team is coming.

---

**You're in initiative. You have the partial cover of the equipment racks. The contractor at the door is acquiring you — they haven't fired yet but they're ten metres away and tracking.**

**You can fire first, fall back deeper toward the secondary panel, or attempt to use the racks as cover to break their sightline. What do you do?**

This is combat. Make a **COMBAT roll** to attack if you're shooting. Your Combat is 30 — roll under on 1d100. Tell me your action and roll the dice.
I want to use the equipment racks as cover and shoot the contractor at the door.

Good cover discipline. You drop into a crouch behind the nearest equipment rack — solid steel frame, deep enough to block centre mass — and bring the rifle up through the gap between two shelving units. It's a tight angle but it's workable. You've shot from worse.

The contractor is still moving into the bay, weapon tracking right. You're left. They haven't acquired you cleanly yet.

You fire first.

**Roll your Combat (roll under 30 on 1d100) — the result will determine whether that 7 damage lands.**

---

While you're rolling, here's what the world does simultaneously:

The contractor squeezes off a burst — but they're firing at where you *were*, not where you are. The rack takes it. Metal shelving punches inward, equipment clatters and skids across the floor, a toolcase detonates off the far wall. Loud. Very loud. But the rounds go wide, chewing up the rack's upper frame instead of you.

Their shot missed. 98 against a Combat of 40 — not even close.

---

From the hub corridor you can now hear two more sets of boots hitting the deck at a run. Twenty seconds out, maybe fifteen. They heard the shot.

The secondary panel is still fifteen metres away on the far wall — the quarantine seal, the purge cycle. Everything you came down here for.

The contractor at the door is reacquiring you through the smoke and scattered debris.

You have one clean shot before they have you in their sights.

**Your Combat roll — 1d100, under 30. The 7 damage is already determined. Hit or miss is yours to decide.**

89. The shot goes wide.

You squeeze the trigger from behind the rack and the round punches into the doorframe a full thirty centimetres left of the contractor — the angle was tighter than you read it, the gap between shelving units eating your peripheral sight picture without you realising until the muzzle flash lit it up wrong. The contractor flinches, instinctively, and that flinch saves them.

They come back up immediately. Professional. They've been shot at before.

Their return burst is wild too — 99, a panicked spray — rounds walking up the ceiling tiles, sparks dropping like slow orange rain in the low gravity, drifting rather than falling. One round clips the top of the rack you're behind and the impact rings through the metal frame into your hands and teeth.

Neither of you has hit anything except furniture.

But the bay is filling with sound. The two sets of boots from the hub corridor — they're in the doorway now, stacking, and you can hear a third voice calling positions in that same clipped shorthand. They're not panicking. They're organising.

You count: one contractor in the bay with you, two more at the door stacking to enter, one unaccounted for. The fourth. Silent. Still somewhere you can't see.

The secondary panel is fifteen metres at your back. The quarantine seal. The purge cycle. Everything you came down here for.

The rack you're behind just took a round through its upper frame. It will not absorb a sustained burst.

You need to move, cover the fifteen metres to the secondary panel, and enter a three-step command sequence — all while three contractors push into this room and a fourth is somewhere you don't know.

The low gravity means debris is still drifting. It also means a hard sprint covers ground differently than you're used to.

**You're pinned behind degraded cover with contacts closing. You can break for the secondary panel now while they're still stacking — it's a dead sprint, fifteen metres, back exposed — or you can hold and try to create a better opening. What do you do?**

If you sprint, that's a **COMBAT roll to cross open ground under fire — roll under 30.**
I feel like I'm committed to the firefight. I try to shoot the contractor again.
I feel like I'm committed to the firefight. I try to shoot the contractor again.

assertion.check: Alvarez's rifle damage (1d10) must not be rolled before her Combat to-hit roll resolves. Original turn rolled the damage (10) before the to-hit roll: "Roll your Combat... If you hit, it's 10 damage."

out-of-order-resolution.situation: Alvarez, already committed to the firefight, tries to shoot the contractor again — her Combat to-hit roll must resolve before any damage roll.
